questions.question: Q1. Define current and the drift velocity relation I = nAvq.
questions.answer: Current is the rate of flow of charge: I = dQ/dt. For a conductor, I = nAvq, where n = charge-carrier density, A = cross-section, v_d = drift velocity, q = charge per carrier.
questions.example: A small drift velocity (mm/s) can carry a large I.

questions.question: Q2. State Ohm's law and define resistivity.
questions.answer: Ohm's law: V = IR (V ∝ I for a conductor at constant temperature), so R = V/I. Resistivity ρ is a material property: R = ρL/A, unit Ω·m; conductivity σ = 1/ρ.

questions.question: Q3. Find the resistance of a 10 m copper wire (ρ = 1.7×10⁻⁸, A = 1 mm²).
Q4. Explain the V–I characteristic of a filament (non-ohmic) vs a wire (ohmic).
questions.answer: An ohmic conductor has a straight-line V–I (R constant); a filament lamp has a curve that flattens at high voltage because its resistance rises with temperature, so it is non-ohmic.
questions.shortcut: Ohmic → straight line; filament → curve (R↑ with T).
questions.example: A diode has an exponential (non-ohmic) V–I.

questions.question: Q5. How do temperature and length affect the resistance of a metal?
questions.answer: For a metal, resistance increases with temperature (higher vibration → more collisions, R = R₀(1+αT)). A longer wire has more resistance (R ∝ L), a thicker one has less (R ∝ 1/A). ▥ 23.1–23.2 Current, Drift Velocity, Resistance & Resistivity  —  Compare / Contrast Tables Resistance vs Resistivity ▣ 23.3–23.6 Series/Parallel, Potential Divider & EMF
questions.shortcut: R ∝ L/A ; metals: R ↑ with T.
questions.example: A long, thin copper wire has high resistance.

questions.question: Q6. State the equivalent resistance for series and for parallel combinations.
questions.answer: Series: R_eq = R₁+R₂+… (same current, add voltages). Parallel: 1/R_eq = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + … (same voltage, currents add).
questions.example: Two 4 Ω in series = 8 Ω; in parallel = 2 Ω.

questions.question: Q7. Three resistors 2, 4, 6 Ω are in parallel. Find R_eq.
Q8. Explain a potential divider and its voltage ratio.
questions.answer: A potential divider divides a supply voltage V across two series resistors R₁ and R₂. The output voltage across R₂ is V₂ = V·R₂/(R₁+R₂), useful to obtain a smaller voltage without drawing much current.
questions.example: R₁=R₂ → output is half the supply.

questions.question: Q9. Define electromotive force (emf) and terminal voltage; relate them.
questions.answer: Emf ε is the energy supplied per unit charge by a source (ideal, no internal loss). Terminal voltage is the usable voltage: V_term = ε − Ir, where r is the internal resistance and I the current. When I=0, V_term = ε.
questions.example: A battery drops terminal V under load (internal r).

questions.question: Q10. A 12 V battery (r=1 Ω) supplies 5 A. Find the terminal voltage.
questions.answer: V_term = ε − Ir = 12 − 5×1 = 7 V. ▥ 23.3–23.6 Series/Parallel, Potential Divider & EMF  —  Compare / Contrast Tables Series vs Parallel Resistance Potential Divider (voltage divider) EMF vs Terminal Potential Difference (in a cell) ▣ 23.7 Work & Power in Electrical Circuits
questions.example: The internal drop is 5 V; only 7 V at the terminals.

questions.question: Q11. Find the power and work done by a current in a resistor.
questions.answer: Power P = IV = I²R = V²/R. Work (heat) in time t: W = Pt = I²Rt (Joule heating). Higher current or resistance dissipates more power as heat.
questions.example: A 4 Ω at 2 A: P = 16 W; in 10 s, 160 J.

questions.question: Q12. A 60 W, 220 V bulb is on for 5 hours. Find the energy and cost (Rs 8/kWh).
Q13. Explain the difference between power and energy in a circuit.
questions.answer: Power is the rate at which energy is transferred (J/s = watt); energy is the total work done over time (J = watt×time). A high-power device transfers energy faster; a long time accumulates a lot of energy even at moderate power. ▥ 23.7 Work & Power in Electrical Circuits  —  Compare / Contrast Tables Work, Power & Energy in DC Circuits PROFESSOR'S THEORY & VIVA BANK   — the kinds of theory a professor / examiner actually asks
questions.shortcut: P (W) vs E (J or kWh) = P×t.
questions.example: A 100 W bulb for 10 h uses 1 kWh of energy.

theoryItems.question: [State] T1. State Ohm's law and define resistivity and conductivity.
theoryItems.answer: Ohm's law: at constant temperature, V ∝ I, so R = V/I. Resistivity ρ (a material property, Ω·m) and conductivity σ = 1/ρ; R = ρL/A, independent of geometry for a given material.

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T2. Explain drift velocity and its relation to current.
theoryItems.answer: Free electrons in a metal move randomly at high speed but, under a field, acquire a small net drift velocity v_d opposite to the field. The current is I = nAv_dq, where n is the carrier density, A the area, q the carrier charge; this relates macroscopic current to microscopic drift.
theoryItems.example: A small v_d (mm/s) can carry a large I.

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T3. Explain the current-voltage characteristic of an ohmic and a non-ohmic device.
theoryItems.answer: An ohmic device (metal wire) has a straight-line V–I (constant R). A non-ohmic device (diode, filament lamp) curves: a diode conducts only above ~0.7 V (Si) in one direction; a filament's resistance rises with temperature, so its V–I flattens at high voltage.
theoryItems.shortcut: Ohmic: straight line; Non-ohmic: curve (diode exponential).
theoryItems.example: A diode has an exponential I–V characteristic.

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T4. Explain resistances in series and in parallel, and the potential divider.
theoryItems.answer: Series: same current, R_eq = R₁+R₂+…; Parallel: same voltage, 1/R_eq = Σ1/R. A potential divider (two series resistors) gives V₂ = V·R₂/(R₁+R₂), producing a smaller, fixed fraction of the supply voltage without drawing much current.
theoryItems.shortcut: Series add; Parallel add reciprocals; divider V₂ = V·R₂/(R₁+R₂).
theoryItems.example: Used to set a reference voltage.

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T5. Explain emf, terminal voltage and internal resistance.
theoryItems.answer: Emf ε is the energy supplied per unit charge by a source (ideal, no internal loss). The terminal voltage is what is available: V_term = ε − Ir, where r is the internal resistance and I the current. Under load the terminal voltage drops; at open circuit (I=0) V_term = ε.
theoryItems.example: A battery 'sags' under heavy current because of its internal r.

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T6. Explain work and power in an electrical circuit, and Joule heating.
theoryItems.answer: Power P = IV = I²R = V²/R; energy W = Pt = I²Rt (Joule heating, lost as heat in a resistor). Higher current or resistance dissipates more power as heat; this is why wires warm and fuses blow when overloaded.
theoryItems.example: A fuse melts when I²Rt exceeds its heat capacity.

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T7. Explain Kirchhoff's rules and apply them to a junction.
theoryItems.answer: Kirchhoff's junction rule: the sum of currents entering a node equals the sum leaving (charge conservation). The loop rule: the algebraic sum of voltages around any closed loop is zero (energy conservation). These let one solve complex circuits by current and potential equations.
theoryItems.example: At a T-junction, current splits; the loop rule balances all drops and emfs.

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T8. Explain a Wheatstone bridge and the balance condition.
theoryItems.answer: A Wheatstone bridge is a network of four resistors forming a diamond with a galvanometer between two opposite points. It is balanced when R₁/R₂ = R₃/R₄ (no current through the galvanometer), letting one find an unknown resistance by adjusting a known one.
theoryItems.example: Used to measure unknown resistances precisely.

theoryItems.question: [Why] T9. Why does a series circuit have higher total resistance than a parallel one?
theoryItems.answer: In series, the same current must pass through every resistor, so the drops add: R_eq = R₁+R₂+… > any single R. In parallel, current divides among several paths, so the equivalent resistance is less than the smallest individual resistor.
theoryItems.shortcut: Series: same I, drops add → R_eq > largest; Parallel: I divides → R_eq < smallest.
theoryItems.example: Adding more parallel resistors always lowers R_eq.

▣ 23.1–23.2 Current, Drift Velocity, Resistance & Resistivity
Q1. Define current and the drift velocity relation I = nAvq.
Answer:  Current is the rate of flow of charge: I = dQ/dt. For a conductor, I = nAvq, where n = charge-carrier density, A = cross-section, v_d = drift velocity, q = charge per carrier.
⚡ Shortcut:  I = nAvq ; v_d = I/(nAq).
Example:  A small drift velocity (mm/s) can carry a large I.
Q2. State Ohm's law and define resistivity.
Answer:  Ohm's law: V = IR (V ∝ I for a conductor at constant temperature), so R = V/I. Resistivity ρ is a material property: R = ρL/A, unit Ω·m; conductivity σ = 1/ρ.
⚡ Shortcut:  R = ρL/A ; σ = 1/ρ.
Example:  Copper ρ ≈ 1.7×10⁻⁸ Ω·m (very conductive).
Q3. Find the resistance of a 10 m copper wire (ρ = 1.7×10⁻⁸, A = 1 mm²).
⚡ Shortcut:  R = ρL/A.
Example:  ≈ 0.17 Ω.
Q4. Explain the V–I characteristic of a filament (non-ohmic) vs a wire (ohmic).
Answer:  An ohmic conductor has a straight-line V–I (R constant); a filament lamp has a curve that flattens at high voltage because its resistance rises with temperature, so it is non-ohmic.
⚡ Shortcut:  Ohmic → straight line; filament → curve (R↑ with T).
Example:  A diode has an exponential (non-ohmic) V–I.
Q5. How do temperature and length affect the resistance of a metal?
Answer:  For a metal, resistance increases with temperature (higher vibration → more collisions, R = R₀(1+αT)). A longer wire has more resistance (R ∝ L), a thicker one has less (R ∝ 1/A).
⚡ Shortcut:  R ∝ L/A ; metals: R ↑ with T.
Example:  A long, thin copper wire has high resistance.

▣ 23.3–23.6 Series/Parallel, Potential Divider & EMF
Q6. State the equivalent resistance for series and for parallel combinations.
Answer:  Series: R_eq = R₁+R₂+… (same current, add voltages). Parallel: 1/R_eq = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + … (same voltage, currents add).
⚡ Shortcut:  Series: add R; Parallel: add 1/R.
Example:  Two 4 Ω in series = 8 Ω; in parallel = 2 Ω.
Q7. Three resistors 2, 4, 6 Ω are in parallel. Find R_eq.
⚡ Shortcut:  1/R_eq = Σ1/Rᵢ.
Example:  ≈ 1.09 Ω.
Q8. Explain a potential divider and its voltage ratio.

Answer:  A potential divider divides a supply voltage V across two series resistors R₁ and R₂. The output voltage across R₂ is V₂ = V·R₂/(R₁+R₂), useful to obtain a smaller voltage without drawing much current.
⚡ Shortcut:  V₂ = V·R₂/(R₁+R₂).
Example:  R₁=R₂ → output is half the supply.
Q9. Define electromotive force (emf) and terminal voltage; relate them.

Answer:  Emf ε is the energy supplied per unit charge by a source (ideal, no internal loss). Terminal voltage is the usable voltage: V_term = ε − Ir, where r is the internal resistance and I the current. When I=0, V_term = ε.
⚡ Shortcut:  V_term = ε − Ir ; r = (ε−V)/I.
Example:  A battery drops terminal V under load (internal r).
Q10. A 12 V battery (r=1 Ω) supplies 5 A. Find the terminal voltage.
Answer:  V_term = ε − Ir = 12 − 5×1 = 7 V.
⚡ Shortcut:  V_term = ε − Ir.
Example:  The internal drop is 5 V; only 7 V at the terminals.

▣ 23.7 Work & Power in Electrical Circuits
Q11. Find the power and work done by a current in a resistor.
Answer:  Power P = IV = I²R = V²/R. Work (heat) in time t: W = Pt = I²Rt (Joule heating). Higher current or resistance dissipates more power as heat.
⚡ Shortcut:  P = I²R = V²/R ; W = Pt.
Example:  A 4 Ω at 2 A: P = 16 W; in 10 s, 160 J.
Q12. A 60 W, 220 V bulb is on for 5 hours. Find the energy and cost (Rs 8/kWh).
Answer:  Energy = P·t = 60×5 = 300 Wh = 0.3 kWh. Cost = 0.3×8 = Rs 2.4. (Energy in J = 300×3600 = 1.08×10⁶ J.)
⚡ Shortcut:  E(kWh) = P(kW)×t(h); cost = kWh×rate.
Example:  0.3 kWh, Rs 2.4.
Q13. Explain the difference between power and energy in a circuit.

Answer:  Power is the rate at which energy is transferred (J/s = watt); energy is the total work done over time (J = watt×time). A high-power device transfers energy faster; a long time accumulates a lot of energy even at moderate power.
⚡ Shortcut:  P (W) vs E (J or kWh) = P×t.
Example:  A 100 W bulb for 10 h uses 1 kWh of energy.

⚡ Short / exam line:  V_term = ε − Ir ; r = (ε−V)/I.

[Explain] T6. Explain work and power in an electrical circuit, and Joule heating.

⚡ Short / exam line:  P = I²R = V²/R ; heat = I²Rt.
Example:  A fuse melts when I²Rt exceeds its heat capacity.
[Explain] T7. Explain Kirchhoff's rules and apply them to a junction.

Answer:  Kirchhoff's junction rule: the sum of currents entering a node equals the sum leaving (charge conservation). The loop rule: the algebraic sum of voltages around any closed loop is zero (energy conservation). These let one solve complex circuits by current and potential equations.
⚡ Short / exam line:  Junction: ΣI_in = ΣI_out ; Loop: ΣV = 0.
Example:  At a T-junction, current splits; the loop rule balances all drops and emfs.

⚡ Short / exam line:  Balance: R₁/R₂ = R₃/R₄.
Example:  Used to measure unknown resistances precisely.
▹ Why  (conceptual & 'why' questions)
[Why] T9. Why does a series circuit have higher total resistance than a parallel one?

Answer:  In series, the same current must pass through every resistor, so the drops add: R_eq = R₁+R₂+… > any single R. In parallel, current divides among several paths, so the equivalent resistance is less than the smallest individual resistor.
⚡ Short / exam line:  Series: same I, drops add → R_eq > largest; Parallel: I divides → R_eq < smallest.
Example:  Adding more parallel resistors always lowers R_eq.
▹ Numerical  (long numericals / problems)
[Numerical] T10. A 12 V source (r = 2 Ω) drives a 6 Ω load. Find the current and terminal voltage.
Answer:  R_total = 6 + 2 = 8 Ω. I = 12/8 = 1.5 A. V_term = ε − Ir = 12 − 1.5×2 = 9 V (or V = IR = 1.5×6 = 9 V).
⚡ Short / exam line:  I = ε/(R+r) ; V_term = IR.
Example:  Current 1.5 A, terminal 9 V.
